source.title: Towards Monosemanticity: Decomposing Language Models With Dictionary Learning

record.file_problem: The supplied text is the full Alignment Forum linkpost and comments, not the longer paper it summarizes.
record.tranche_reason: Reports dictionary-learning feature results in a language model, extending evidence about superposition-related representations to an LLM setting.
record.gate_note: The post reports qualitative results for feature decomposition, interpretability, cross-model universality, and resolution. The comments are not treated as the study's results. The post mentions steering but gives no specific outcome measure, and steering is deliberately induced; it is not counted as evidence that the features naturally arise. It also mentions neuron examples, but does not test the capacity account or show that polysemanticity arises without capacity pressure.
record.test_reason: The post reports its own dictionary-learning results on a small transformer LM. These are evidence on V4: sparse, interpretable features are recovered that neurons do not show. They also bear on V5 through cross-model universality and the dependence of the features on dictionary size. This is not an original source.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors also say features are better units of analysis than neurons, and that the next obstacle to interpreting large models is engineering rather than science.
record.recipe_differences: Dictionary learning on language-model activations and qualitative feature evaluation, rather than the original toy-model experiments on feature geometry. This is a linkpost summary of a research paper.
record.method_sensitivity: The number of learned features changes the decomposition's resolution and interpretability.
record.problems: The post omits model names, numerical scores, sample sizes, and uncertainty estimates for the reported comparisons. It summarizes a longer paper rather than giving the full experimental detail, and its reported model is small.

untested.parts: All of it: no toy-model geometry or sparsity transition.
All of it: no test of capacity competition.
Larger or frontier models; quantitative spread of features across neurons.
Completeness of the dictionary (reconstruction loss is not reported in the post).

missing.what: Neuron polysemanticity example: one neuron fires on academic citations, English dialogue, HTTP requests and Korean text. This is direct evidence on features being spread across neurons.
missing.locator: Main post, paragraph beginning 'Unfortunately, it turns out that the individual neurons'

missing.what: Human interpretability rubric values (median neuron 0, median feature 12). These are quoted from the paper in a comment.

record.verdict_notes: This is a linkpost summary; the full paper (Towards Monosemanticity) has quantitative results that are not in this text. The steering result is correctly excluded because it is induced on purpose. Comments are not treated as study results, except to point to the missing rubric numbers.

versions.untested_parts: Toy-model feature geometry, sparsity-dependent transitions, and regular arrangements.
Whether limited capacity causes polysemanticity or whether important features receive dedicated dimensions.
Whether polysemanticity can arise without capacity pressure, and whether it is evidence of superposition.
The post gives results for a small language model, not frontier-scale models; it does not quantify the extent to which features are distributed across neurons.
Whether SAE features are complete or canonical; the post reports qualitative universality and resolution changes, not comprehensive tests of feature stability.
Whether represented features are one-dimensional directions rather than multidimensional features.

rows.subject: a transformer language model
rows.operation_detail: Decomposed layer activations with dictionary learning into features.
rows.locator: Main post, paragraph beginning “In a transformer language model”
rows.note: The model and layer are not named in the post.
rows.check: The count of 'more than 4000 features' is the dictionary size the researchers chose, not a measured quantity. The finding the row should record is that the learned features represent properties invisible in individual neurons (DNA, legal text, Hebrew and others).

rows.subject: human evaluator
rows.operation_detail: Blinded human evaluator scored feature and neuron interpretability.
rows.value: features have much higher scores than neurons
rows.locator: Main post, paragraph beginning “To validate that the features”
rows.note: No scores or sample sizes are given in the post.
rows.check: The post gives no numbers. A comment quotes the paper: median neuron rubric 0 vs median feature 12. That is not in the post body.

rows.subject: another model
rows.operation_detail: Scored feature and neuron descriptions by predicting feature activations from descriptions.
rows.locator: Main post, paragraph beginning “We additionally take an ‘autointerpretability’ approach”
rows.note: The scoring model and numerical results are not stated.
rows.check: No numbers given; the row is fine as qualitative.

rows.subject: features learned in different models
rows.operation_detail: Compared learned feature sets across models.
rows.value: features are largely universal between different models
rows.locator: Main post, paragraph beginning “Finally, we zoom out”
rows.note: The post gives no model names, quantitative measure, or detailed description of the comparison.
rows.check: 'Largely universal' is stated as a positive finding, so it is observed rather than partial. It is qualitative only: no models or metric are named.

rows.subject: a transformer language model
rows.operation_detail: Tuned the number of learned features.
rows.measure: Resolution and interpretability of the decomposition
rows.value: A small set of features gives a coarse view that is easier to understand.
rows.locator: Main post, paragraph beginning “Finally, we zoom out”
rows.note: The result describes a resolution tradeoff rather than establishing a single canonical feature set.
rows.check: r5 and r6 describe one result: the feature set changes with dictionary size (feature splitting). They could be merged. Against V5's 'canonical units' claim, this shows the units depend on a hyperparameter.

rows.subject: a transformer language model
rows.operation_detail: Tuned the number of learned features.
rows.measure: Resolution and interpretability of the decomposition
rows.value: A large set of features gives a more refined view that reveals subtle model properties.
rows.locator: Main post, paragraph beginning “Finally, we zoom out”
rows.note: The post describes different granularities as useful; it does not establish that the larger set is complete or canonical.
rows.check: Same result as r5; see r5.

relationships.condition: small (one-layer) transformer, MLP layer of 512 neurons
relationships.reason: The SAE recovers features rated far more interpretable than neurons by blinded humans and by autointerpretability (r1–r3).
relationships.display_finding: Blinded human raters and autointerpretability both rated SAE features far more interpretable than neurons.

relationships.reason: The post states the learned features are largely universal between models; this is qualitative only (r4).
relationships.display_finding: The post states that the learned features are largely universal between models, without a quantitative measure.

relationships.condition: varying the number of learned features
relationships.reason: The decomposition changes with dictionary size, from coarse to refined, so there is no single canonical feature set (r5, r6).
relationships.display_finding: Increasing the number of learned features refined the decomposition from coarse to fine, so there was no single canonical feature set.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
